item.title: Summary of Key Policy Rate Discussion by NBU Monetary Policy Committee on 28 October 2026
item.description:
Meeting date: 28 October 2026.

Attendees: all 11 members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the National Bank of Ukraine:

  • Andriy Pyshnyy, Governor of the National Bank of Ukraine
  • Sergiy Nikolaychuk, First Deputy Governor
  • Volodymyr Lepushynskyi, Deputy Governor
  • Yuriy Heletiy, Deputy Governor
  • Yaroslav Matuzka, Deputy Governor
  • Dmytro Oliinyk, Deputy Governor
  • Oleksii Shaban, Deputy Governor
  • Taras Tokarchuk, Director, Monetary Policy and Economic Analysis Department
  • Pervin Dadashova, Director, Financial Stability Department
  • Oleksandr Arseniuk, Director, Open Market Operations Department
  • Yuriy Polovniov, Director, Statistics and Reporting Department.

Members of the MPC discussed the main drivers of mounting price pressures, as well as changes in the distribution of risks to future inflation developments and economic activity. Considerable attention was devoted to assessing the optimal level of monetary conditions that would ensure a sustained slowdown in inflation toward the 5% target while not creating undue obstacles to lending and economic recovery

Price pressures continue to intensify, MPC members said during the discussion. In September 2026, consumer inflation accelerated significantly (to 10% yoy), substantially exceeding the NBU’s July forecast (8.4% yoy). Higher fuel prices, as well as intensified russian attacks on production, storage, and logistics infrastructure, exerted upward pressure on the prices of a wide range of raw and processed food products. As a result, core inflation also picked up (to 8.8% yoy), exceeding the NBU’s July forecast (8.3% yoy). By NBU estimates, both headline and core inflation continued to rise in October.

The intensification of inflationary pressures and their spread across a wider range of goods and services were accompanied by a deterioration in inflation expectations. Households’ inflation expectations remained volatile and elevated. Financial analysts gradually revised their expectations upward, from 7.5% in June to 8.8% in October. Banks’ inflation expectations also increased, from 8.7% in July to 10% in October.

The large-scale destruction and higher energy prices also led to a cooling of economic activity and the labor market. The adverse impact of the deteriorating security situation was only partially offset by a significant loosening of fiscal policy and relatively favorable conditions in the energy sector. As a result, real GDP declined in Q3, business sentiment deteriorated across all types of economic activity, and demand for workers declined in some sectors and regions. At the same time, these trends did not have a significant dampening effect on overall price dynamics. Consumer demand continued to grow, albeit at a slower pace. Household incomes were supported both by rising real wages amid the still-high labor shortages and by an expansion of fiscal stimulus.

At the same time, pressure on the FX market intensified. Significant losses of production capacity and the blockade of seaports severely constrained the ability of exporters, primarily agricultural producers and metals-and-mining companies, to export. Meanwhile, imports increased amid high demand for energy, energy equipment, and machinery products for the defense industrial base. As a result, the private sector’s FX deficit widened, and the NBU increased its FX sales interventions to offset it.

The balance of risks to price developments remained tilted upward. On the one hand, Ukraine’s fulfillment of a number of commitments to its international partners reduced uncertainty about the regularity and adequacy of official financing in the coming periods. On the other hand, risks associated with the consequences of russia’s aerial terror campaign intensified. The risks of global energy prices persisting at elevated levels for an extended period due to the war in the Middle East also remained significant.

Eight MPC members supported raising the key policy rate to 16.5% in October

These discussion participants agreed that tighter interest rate policy is necessary amid a significant increase in price pressures and a notable deterioration in inflation expectations. The NBU must demonstrate through its actions, not words, its readiness to ensure price stability in order to minimize the risks of inflation expectations becoming unanchored and inflation remaining entrenched at high levels for a protracted period. Raising the key policy rate to 16.5% will accelerate the transmission of previous policy steps and help maintain the attractiveness of hryvnia-denominated assets, which is an important prerequisite for ensuring FX market sustainability and containing inflation. This decision is also consistent with the NBU’s September forward guidance and is the most widely expected outcome according to surveys of market participants. It may therefore also help contain price pressures through the expectations channel.

Inflation has been rising faster than expected in recent months despite the cooling of the economy, several discussion participants noted. The combination of supply-side inflationary shocks and weakening economic activity creates a difficult dilemma for monetary policy. If such shocks are transitory, the central bank can afford greater flexibility and refrain from tightening interest rate policy, provided inflation expectations remain under control. However, the current situation in Ukraine appears to be different in terms of both the transitory nature of the shock and its impact on expectations.

Second-round effects of higher fuel prices and rising business production costs, which may turn out to be more significant than the NBU expected, are now playing a key role in accelerating inflation, one of these MPC members emphasized. High energy prices, significant wage increases amid labor shortages, higher logistics costs, and inventory losses caused by russian attacks are feeding through into higher prices across a broad range of goods. For example, the share of the consumer basket items with price increases exceeding 10% rose from 42% in August to 48% in September. The share of core inflation components whose price growth rates exceed their average over the past five years increased from 26% in June to 33% in September. Seasonally adjusted annualized rates of both headline and core inflation also rose sharply. Ignoring the persistent inflationary trend because of scattered signs of cooling domestic demand would be short-sighted. That choice could raise the cost of bringing inflation back to its target in the future, this MPC member said. Instead, raising the key policy rate is justified to contain underlying price pressures.

Another MPC member pointed to worrying trends in inflation expectations. Households’ inflation expectations, though inherently volatile, have remained in double digits for a prolonged period and have been gradually increasing. The information environment has stayed negative after escalated russian strikes, raising the risk that inflation expectations become unanchored. At the same time, in recent months, professional survey respondents’ inflation expectations have increasingly exceeded the NBU’s forecast. Although banks and financial analysts are usually less sensitive to the information environment, their inflation forecasts have also worsened. All this shows that the NBU needs to act to reaffirm its commitment to its price stability mandate. Raising the key policy rate to 16.5% will not only strengthen the effects of previous decisions but also serve as an important signaling tool and help stabilize inflation expectations.

Another discussion participant agreed, noting that, according to the latest surveys, most financial market participants expect the NBU to raise the key policy rate. Moreover, the share of respondents who view tighter interest rate policy as appropriate rose noticeably in October compared with previous months. This indicates growing concern among economic agents about price trends. Given that the NBU has also revised its inflation forecast for 2026–2027 upward, a failure to deliver an adequate monetary policy response would have an additional adverse impact on inflation expectations.

As another MPC member noted, the NBU’s delay in tightening monetary policy could, among other things, increase the risks of triggering a wage-price spiral. If inflation expectations continue to worsen, businesses will pass costs on to prices more actively, while employees will demand significantly higher wages to compensate for losses in their purchasing power. This will make it harder to bring inflation back to target even after the direct effects of energy and other supply shocks have abated. Under these circumstances, it is important for the NBU to act preemptively, without waiting for the risks to fully materialize and feed through into actual inflation. The timing of policy decisions is crucial, as a prompt response by the central bank always minimizes the need for significantly tighter policy going forward.

An important reason to raise the key policy rate is the need to ensure that hryvnia assets remain sufficiently attractive as a means of saving, another MPC member noted. With inflation expectations deteriorating, real returns on these instruments are declining. Increased pressure on the hryvnia exchange rate, driven by lower exports and substantial demand for defense-related imports, could also weaken incentives to hold term savings in the national currency. The NBU needs to respond to these developments by preventing a shift of hryvnia savings and funds held in current accounts into the FX market. Raising the key policy rate will help increase real returns on hryvnia instruments and contain pressure on the FX market, which is particularly important during a period of heavy budgetary spending.

Tightening interest rate policy to reduce inflation is consistent with the NBU’s intention to support the economy, several discussion participants pointed out. Price stability is a necessary prerequisite for the economy to return to sustainable growth and for lending to develop on a sound footing. A moderate increase in the key policy rate will not have a significant restrictive effect on lending. Despite the key policy rate increases in July and September, lending growth has remained steady. In addition, the NBU remains focused on further supporting lending to sectors critical to strengthening defense capabilities and economic resilience. In recent months, the NBU has adopted four packages of regulatory changes aimed, among other things, at supporting businesses in the defense, energy, agriculture, and trade sectors. It is important to continue providing such support.

Three MPC members supported keeping the key policy rate unchanged at 16% in October

They believe that previous interest rate policy tightening has already ensured sufficiently tight monetary conditions to contain price pressures. At the same time, the NBU’s proactive stance has created room for a more flexible response to current adverse economic trends resulting from russian attacks. There is a high probability of a sustained cooling in business activity and the labor market, which could lead to a faster easing of price pressures than projected in the NBU’s current forecast, these MPC members said. In light of this, it would be preferable to refrain from further increasing the key policy rate for now and instead preserve stronger incentives for lending growth and, consequently, economic support.

Signs of weaker domestic demand have become much more pronounced compared with the previous MPC meeting, one of these discussion participants emphasized. The deteriorating security situation and frequent air raid alerts have been significantly constraining consumer activity. This is evidenced, among other things, by slower growth in retail trade. At the same time, retail trade would have been even weaker had it not been for active household purchases of goods, including fuel, power equipment, and medications, in preparation for winter and potential disruptions to energy supplies. Amid escalated russian bombardments, businesses’ demand for new workers has also declined, while some companies whose production and storage facilities have been damaged by air strikes have resorted to targeted staff cuts. This could curb wage growth and consumer demand, thereby also limiting price pressures. Under these circumstances, an additional increase in the key policy rate could prove excessive.

A 0.5 pp increase in the key policy rate would serve as a signal to shape expectations but would hardly have a significant impact on consumer price dynamics toward the end of the year, another MPC member said. The inflation spike has already largely materialized, while further price pressures will be driven primarily by supply-side factors, which are likely to start fading in early 2027. In particular, this participant expects the active phase of the war in the Middle East to end in H1 2027, which would help stabilize fuel prices at lower levels. Meanwhile, businesses’ rapid adaptation to the effects of air strikes, including restructuring logistics and decentralizing storage facilities, will help limit the risk of localized goods shortages and sustain adequate supply going forward. Another factor that could contain price pressures is an increase in domestic food supply, given the difficulties of exporting it.

The NBU has built up a certain buffer of resilience through decisive steps in previous months and can now afford to take a wait-and-see approach to assess the situation more carefully, another participant noted. Household investments in hryvnia assets have continued to grow in recent months, including a rising share of term deposits in the banking system. This suggests the NBU’s earlier policy steps have worked. Overall, monetary conditions remain tight enough to sustain demand for hryvnia deposits and domestic government debt securities, which, among other things, will help restrain consumption and a shift of savings into foreign currency. Even without raising the key policy rate in October, you can expect further increases in hryvnia deposit rates, as monetary transmission works with a delay and not all banks have yet adjusted their rates in response to the NBU’s previous steps. The sustained growth in household investments in hryvnia deposits and domestic government debt securities, together with the remaining potential for monetary transmission, suggests that the NBU should not rush into further tightening of interest rate policy, this MPC member said. In December, the NBU will make its decision when there is more information available to assess how persistent the economic slowdown is and what impact it is having on inflation.

Discussion participants expect a moderate easing of interest rate policy in 2027 as risks to price developments and inflation expectations subside

Given the significant increase in price pressures and the worsening of inflation expectations, none of the MPC members sees room to cut the key policy rate in the coming months. Most of them also see risks of an upward shift in the key policy rate trajectory relative to the NBU’s current forecast. At the same time, discussion participants agreed that in 2027 the NBU would likely be able to ease interest rate policy as inflation slows and the risk of inflation expectations becoming unanchored diminishes.

MPC members expect a gradual and prudent reduction in the key policy rate in 2027, to around 14%. At the same time, they agreed that the NBU would respond flexibly to actual developments and further changes in the distribution of risks, taking into account both persistent price pressures and the possible impact of weaker economic activity.

For reference

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is an NBU advisory body that was created to share information and opinions on monetary policy formulation and implementation in order to deliver price stability. The MPC comprises the NBU Governor, NBU Board members, and directors of the Monetary Policy and Economic Analysis Department, Open Market Operations Department, Financial Stability Department, and Statistics and Reporting Department. The MPC meets the day before the NBU Board meeting on monetary policy issues.

Decisions on monetary policy issues are made by the NBU Board.

item.title: NBU Supports Stable Operation of Ukraine’s Energy System
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has extended the maximum settlement deadlines for payments for natural gas imports by authorized state-owned companies to 365 days, in line with proposals received from the government of Ukraine (Ordinance No. 1089 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine On Amendments to Ordinance No. 76 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine dated 13 February 2019 dated 21 October 2026).

Following consultations with the Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine, the NBU is extending the maximum settlement deadline from 180 to 365 days for transactions involving imports of goods classified under code 2711210000 (natural gas) according to the Ukrainian Classification of Goods for Foreign Economic Activity (UCGFEA), provided that such transactions are carried out by a natural gas market participant whose shares (stakes) are 100% owned directly or indirectly by the state and that such a participant has been assigned special obligations by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine pursuant to Article 11 of the Law of Ukraine On the Natural Gas Market to ensure the public interest in the functioning of the natural gas market. This extended settlement deadline will apply to transactions carried out from 9 November 2026.

Extending the maximum settlement deadline will contribute to the country’s energy security. It will enable companies responsible for building up natural gas reserves for the supply of consumers in Ukraine to procure imported natural gas on the most favorable and competitive terms. This will ease pressure on the FX market.

These amendments were approved by NBU Board Resolution No. 127 On Amendments to NBU Board Resolution No. 67 dated 14 May 2019 dated 6 November 2026, which takes effect on 7 November 2026.

For reference

In line with the Law of Ukraine On Currency and Currency Operations, the NBU is authorized to independently set only general settlement deadlines for export and import transactions for all enterprises, regardless of their ownership structure or industry. Currently, pursuant to NBU Board Resolution No. 18 On Operation of Banking System Under Martial Law dated 24 February 2022 (as amended), settlements shall be made within 180 calendar days (for transactions conducted on or after 5 April 2022). 

At the same time, this law delineates the respective powers of the NBU and the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine in special cases. The NBU is authorized to establish (extend or reduce) settlement deadlines for specific sectors or goods that differ from the general settlement deadlines solely on the basis of informed recommendations from the government.

item.title: Keeping in Touch with Businesses: NBU Meets with Heads of Ukrainian Companies Participating in Its Surveys
item.description:
On 4 November 2026, the NBU held an online meeting with heads of Ukrainian companies participating in its business outlook surveys.

These regular meetings, held twice a year, provide a platform for constructive dialogue with businesses. They offer an opportunity to communicate the NBU’s decisions and outline its near-term plans, answer pressing questions and provide expert explanations, as well as receive feedback and proposals from the business community.

The event brought together 113 representatives of 110 companies from various sectors of economic activity and the vast majority of Ukraine’s regions.

In his opening remarks, NBU Deputy Governor Volodymyr Lepushynskyi thanked Ukrainian businesses for their extraordinary resilience and adaptability to the challenges of the war, as well as for participating in the NBU’s surveys.

“Maintaining regular contact with businesses is very important to the NBU. Analyzing the results of business surveys alongside other data enables us to cross-check information promptly, see the overall picture of the economy, identify risks in a timely manner, and respond to them appropriately,” Volodymyr Lepushynskyi noted.

The meeting’s agenda traditionally covered a wide range of issues, including an overview of the current state of the economy and the NBU’s revised macroeconomic forecast, interest rate policy and developments in the FX market, the priorities and results of FX liberalization, support for businesses from the banking sector, and more.

Economic overview and macroeconomic forecast

In September, headline inflation accelerated to 10.0% yoy, while core inflation rose to 8.8% yoy. According to the NBU’s preliminary estimates, these trends continued in October.

The escalation of russia’s targeted air strikes on production, storage, and logistics infrastructure, as well as the direct and second-round effects of higher fuel prices, are driving up production costs and reducing the supply of goods and services.

The NBU raised its inflation forecast for 2026 to 12.5%. The effects of bombardments alone will add around 0.7 pp to annual inflation. In 2027, inflation will slow to 7.3% yoy. This will be supported, in particular, by the NBU’s interest rate policy measures aimed at maintaining the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and FX market sustainability. Inflation is expected to return to the 5% target in 2028.

Economic activity declined in Q3 2026. The main factors were escalated russian attacks on production capacity and logistics, as well as the blockade of ports. The metallurgy and ore mining industries suffered the greatest losses. Performance also deteriorated in other industrial sectors, wholesale trade, and agriculture. Business outlook fell to their lowest level since Q3 2024. The negative impact was partially mitigated by substantial budget expenditures, high yields of certain crops, and the absence of an electricity deficit.

The NBU revised its forecast for real GDP growth in 2026 downward, to a negative 0.4%. The deterioration in the forecast was driven primarily by the effects of intensified bombardments, whose contribution to GDP is estimated at a negative 1.9 pp. In 2027, the economy may grow by 0.4%, provided the NBU’s technical assumption of improved logistics starting in the middle of next year materializes. As security risks decline, economic growth is expected to accelerate to 2.2% in 2028.

A comprehensive overview of the macroeconomic forecast is provided in the October 2026 Inflation Report.

Interest rate and exchange rate policy

In view of a significant increase in price pressures and a deterioration in inflation expectations, the NBU raised its key policy rate to 16.5% in October. This prudent decision makes it possible to maintain a balance between controlling inflation and supporting the economy. This step will help preserve the attractiveness of hryvnia assets and FX market sustainability, thereby keeping inflation expectations and price dynamics under control.

The forecast envisages keeping the key policy rate at its current level through Q2 2027. At the same time, the NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the distribution of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and the possible effects of weaker economic activity.

Under the current managed flexibility exchange rate regime, exchange rate dynamics are determined primarily by market trends, namely changes in the balance of FX supply and demand. Exchange rate flexibility works in both directions, meaning that the hryvnia can either depreciate or appreciate depending on market developments. The NBU does not seek to maintain the exchange rate within a particular corridor or at a particular level.

Ukraine has operated under the managed flexibility exchange rate regime since October 2023. This regime is designed around the realities of a wartime economy. To meet its pan-European security commitments, Ukraine receives substantial financial assistance from international partners. This financing makes it possible to cover the budget deficit, which has increased severalfold due to the full-scale war. International assistance does not enter the FX market directly: the government sells the foreign currency it receives to the NBU. The NBU acts as an intermediary in the FX market, balancing the hryvnia supply entering the market through budget expenditures with FX interventions.

Thus, the managed flexibility exchange rate regime makes it possible to limit the impact on exchange rate formation of the portion of budget expenditures financed by international assistance.

The NBU’s actions in the FX market are guided by the principles of the flexible inflation targeting regime, which, on the one hand, relies on FX interventions as one of the instruments for ensuring price stability and, on the other, is aimed at gradually increasing the role of the exchange rate as a shock absorber.

Maintaining FX market sustainability is important for the NBU to fulfill its primary mandate of ensuring price stability. To this end, the NBU has all the necessary instruments and sufficient international reserves.

Easing FX Restrictions

FX liberalization is a systematic process being pursued under the Strategy for Easing FX Restrictions, Transitioning to Greater Flexibility of the Exchange Rate, and Returning to Inflation Targeting. Its overall rationale and sequencing are set out in the Roadmap for Easing FX Restrictions. The ultimate goal is to return to FX regulation based on the principles that were in place before the full-scale war.

Implementation of the Roadmap measures significantly improves the business and financial sector environment, helps households meet their basic needs, diversify their savings, and develop an investment culture.

In October, the NBU published the Interim Stocktaking Report on Measures to Liberalize the FX Market. Current business transactions have now been largely liberalized, and exporters have been given certain opportunities to hedge FX risks. Economic incentives have also been introduced to attract new investment and loans. Foreign investors can invest in the capital of Ukrainian companies or provide loans and, where necessary, repatriate profits and receive their own payments for loan repayment and servicing.

The package of measures for stimulative liberalization also includes incentives to attract new capital. Businesses can conduct important transactions above the limits under the investment, donation, loan, and charitable contribution categories. Businesses can also share certain limits with affiliated companies.

The total volume of transactions under stimulative liberalization currently stands at USD 1,110 million, while the available unused limit (the amount of funds that have not yet been transferred abroad within the available limits) stands at USD 1,198 million.

FX market liberalization remains a priority for the NBU. It should continue to be comprehensive, covering different groups and categories, including businesses, households, and the financial sector.

The NBU maintains an ongoing dialogue with the government, international organizations, business associations, and experts to identify the most pressing needs regarding the easing of FX restrictions. The results of these consultations are taken into account when structuring subsequent packages of FX liberalization measures.

The next steps will be taken gradually, subject to the availability of the necessary macroeconomic prerequisites and taking into account the priorities identified, including attracting new investment into the Ukrainian economy.

During the meeting, NBU representatives – experts from the Statistics and Reporting Department, Monetary Policy and Economic Analysis Department, Financial Stability Department, Open Market Operations Department, and Department of Methodology for Nonbank Financial Institutions – provided detailed answers to questions from representatives of the business community.

In his closing remarks, Yurii Polovnov, Director of the NBU’s Statistics and Reporting Department, thanked the meeting participants for the constructive dialogue and their active participation in the NBU’s surveys, which are an important source of information about the functioning of the economy, business sentiment, and expectations.

As usual, we invite business representatives to take part in monthly online surveys through the NBU’s Business Outlook Surveys mobile app. It can be downloaded from Google Play and the App Store.

The NBU will continue to hold regular meetings with heads of companies participating in its business outlook surveys.

item.title: Inflation to Accelerate through End of 2026, but to Return to Downward Path as Early as 2027 – Inflation Report
item.description:
The NBU has published its October Inflation Report, which provides a detailed analysis and forecast of the macroeconomic situation. The forecast is based on the assumption that Ukraine will fulfill its commitments under cooperation programs with international partners, which will provide financial support in the necessary amounts. Other important technical assumptions underlying the forecast include improved logistics starting in mid-2027 and a gradual decline in security risks toward the end of the forecast horizon. The forecast takes into account the damage already inflicted by russian attacks, although the risks of further losses remain high.

According to the NBU’s forecast, inflation will accelerate to 12.5% in 2026 before starting to decline next year, reaching 7.3% at the end of 2027 and 5% in 2028. Real GDP will contract by 0.4% this year, grow by 0.4% in 2027, and by 2.2% in 2028.

Inflation will accelerate in the coming months, but start declining in 2027

Consumer inflation will pick up to 12.5% in 2026. Higher fuel prices and the effects of damage to production and logistics infrastructure will continue to increase businesses’ costs and feed through to prices via both direct and second-round effects. In addition, price pressures will intensify amid the expected expansion of fiscal stimulus toward the end of the year.

Inflation is projected to decline to 7.3% in 2027 and to the target of 5% in 2028. Price pressures will gradually ease as the effects of higher fuel prices dissipate and wage growth slows amid subdued economic activity. The NBU’s monetary policy measures will also have a significant impact.

From July through October 2026, the NBU raised its key policy rate from 15% to 16.5% to maintain the attractiveness of hryvnia savings, ease pressure on the FX market, and keep inflation expectations under control. The NBU stands ready to respond flexibly to further changes in the distribution of risks, taking into account both the persistence of price pressures and the impact of weaker economic activity on inflation processes.

Intensified attacks constrain the economy’s potential and hold back economic recovery

According to the NBU’s forecast, real GDP will decline by 0.4% in 2026. The effects of large-scale destruction of production, energy, and logistics infrastructure will be only partially offset by increased fiscal stimulus toward the end of the year.

Losses in economic potential will also continue to constrain economic recovery in 2027–2028. At the same time, the NBU’s forecast envisages real GDP growth of 0.4% in 2027, driven by increased public investment in the defense industrial base and the restoration of critical infrastructure. In 2028, economic growth may accelerate to 2.2% amid a pickup in consumer demand, higher harvests, and increased private investment as security risks decline.

Labor shortages will persist, while wage growth will continue despite slowing

As economic activity weakens, businesses’ demand for workers has declined. However, the overall labor shortage persists due to mobilization and migration. The NBU’s forecast assumes net population outflow of around 0.2 million people annually in 2026–2027. At the same time, a net return of approximately 0.1 million migrants is expected in 2028 as security risks decline and economic conditions improve.

Structural labor shortages will continue to drive wage growth, although its pace will gradually slow. Real wages are expected to increase by 11.4% in 2026. At the same time, their growth will slow to 4%–5% per year in 2027–2028.

The NBU expects international assistance to be sufficient to finance the budget deficit without resorting to monetary financing, while also enabling further accumulation of international reserves

The NBU’s forecast envisages an increase in the budget deficit (excluding grants from revenues) to around 35% of GDP in 2026 and around 37% in 2027. It is subsequently expected to gradually narrow to 20% of GDP in 2028.

International assistance will remain the key source of budget deficit financing. In 2026, Ukraine is expected to receive around USD 50 billion in direct budget financing, followed by more than USD 52 billion in 2027 and USD 44 billion in 2028. In addition, Ukraine is expected to receive funds under the defense component of the Ukraine Support Loan program: more than USD 32 billion this year and USD 37 billion next year.

Thanks to international support, international reserves will exceed USD 62 billion at the end of 2026 and 2027, and will amount to around USD 57 billion in 2028.

In addition to updated macroeconomic forecasts, the October Inflation Report features several special topic boxes:

Impact of Escalated russian Attacks on Businesses and Infrastructure

The intensification of russian strikes on businesses and infrastructure, combined with the blockade of ports, has led to a sharp slowdown in economic activity and increased price pressures. By NBU estimates, the combined negative effect of these developments in Q3–Q4 2026 will result in real GDP being 1.9 pp lower in 2026 than it would have been in their absence, while annual inflation will be 0.7 pp higher. Losses in the balance of trade will reach USD 6.6 billion, primarily due to a decline in agricultural exports. The adverse effects on economic activity and price dynamics stemming from russian air strikes will also be felt in 2027.

Increased inflationary pressures will require the NBU to maintain sufficiently tight monetary conditions to preserve the attractiveness of hryvnia savings and keep both inflation expectations and exchange rate expectations under control. The main priority will remain ensuring a steady decline in inflation toward the 5% target, while the NBU will also take into account weaker economic activity and domestic demand when making its decisions.

How Big Data and AI Help Inform Monetary Policy Decisions

Big data and artificial intelligence have significantly expanded the NBU’s analytical capabilities amid unprecedented uncertainty caused by the full-scale war and its consequences. Alternative data enable the NBU to compensate for gaps in and delays to official statistics, while news analysis and synthetic surveys make it possible to identify changes in economic agents’ sentiment more promptly.

At the same time, expert judgment remains an important element of analytical work: the NBU cross-checks new indicators against official data and incorporates them into its decision-making process only through its macroeconomic forecast, while retaining control over the data and models. Combining new technologies with expert judgment makes it possible to identify signs of economic shocks earlier, maintain the consistency of monetary policy, and communicate the NBU’s decisions more effectively.

item.title: Banks Have Sufficient Foreign Cash Holdings: Results of FX Cash Supply Transactions
item.description:
As announced, on 5 November 2026, the National Bank of Ukraine conducted transactions to exchange banks’ cashless foreign currency for foreign currency cash to replenish their cash holdings.

Banks’ demand for such transactions remains moderate, indicating that the financial system has sufficient stocks of foreign cash.

The results of the NBU’s transactions to supply banks with foreign currency cash on 5 November are as follows:

  • total declared volume of transactions – USD 50 million and EUR 50 million
  • number of participants – four banks
  • total volume of requests – USD 40 million and EUR 9 million
  • demand has been met in full.

Overall, based on results of 3–5 November 2026, the volume of foreign currency offered within these transactions significantly exceeded the actual demand from banks.

The NBU stands ready to continue its efforts to maintain the sustainability of the foreign exchange market, including by conducting additional operations, if necessary, to replenish banks’ cash stocks with foreign currency cash. At the same time, the financial system currently has sufficient FX cash liquidity to meet the needs of Ukrainians.

For reference

The NBU’s transactions to exchange banks’ cashless foreign currency for foreign currency cash to replenish their foreign cash holdings do not affect the volume of Ukraine’s international reserves in any way.

item.title: International Reserves Increase to USD 49.1 Billion in October
item.description:
According to preliminary data, Ukraine had USD 49,075.8 million in international reserves as of 1 November 2026. In October, international reserves increased by 4.2% thanks to FX inflows from international partners, which exceeded the NBU’s net FX sales, and Ukraine’s FX debt repayments. International reserves are sufficient for maintaining FX market sustainability.

In general, several factors determined the dynamics of international reserves in October 2026.

First, inflows to the government’s accounts and the servicing and repayment of public debt

In October, a total of USD 3,690.5 million came into the government's FX accounts with the NBU, where:

  • USD 3,285.9 million from the European Union
  • USD 404.6 million via World Bank accounts.

Furthermore, Ukraine received USD 4.6 billion from the EU of the defense tranche under Ukraine Support Loan. These funds were not included into Ukraine’s international reserves due to restricted (targeted) use of the funds. However, if the government sells these funds to the NBU for hryvnia for further targeted use, international reserves will increase by the respective amount. In October, the government converted USD 4.6 billion into hryvnia contributing to the increase in international reserves. At the same time, it should be noted that hryvnia funding at the cost of these funds increases demand in the FX market effecting the scale of the NBU’s FX interventions. So, such NBU operations cause redistribution of these funds.

A total of USD 242.3 million was spent on servicing and repaying the FX public debt, including:

  • USD 197.9 million to service and repay the debt to the World Bank
  • USD 7.2 million to service FX domestic government debt securities
  • USD 37.2 million to meet the country’s liabilities to other creditors.

In addition, Ukraine repaid USD 252.8 million to the International Monetary Fund.

Second, the NBU’s transactions in the Ukrainian FX market

In October, the NBU sold USD 6,051.2 million and purchased USD 0.4 million in the FX market, according to balance sheet data. The NBU was a net seller of USD 6,050.8 million.

Third, the revaluation of financial instruments (due to changes in their market value and exchange rate fluctuations) and the impact of other factors.

International reserves increased by USD 204.4 million in October due to revaluation of financial instruments and other factors.

International reserves are now covering 4.2 months of future imports.

Data on international reserves and FX liquidity are compiled and released on a monthly basis:  

  • for preliminary data, no later than on the 7th day after the reporting month ends
  • for revised data, no later than on the 21st day after the reporting month ends.

Revised data are available here.

item.title: Banks Have Sufficient Foreign Cash Holdings: Results of FX Cash Supply Transactions
item.description:
As announced, on 4 November 2026, the National Bank of Ukraine conducted preventive transactions to exchange banks’ non-cash foreign currency for cash foreign currency to replenish their cash holdings. Banks’ demand for such transactions remains moderate, indicating that the financial system has sufficient stocks of foreign cash.

The results of the NBU’s transactions to supply banks with foreign currency cash on 4 November are as follows:

  • total declared volume of transactions – USD 50 million and EUR 50 million
  • number of participants – four banks
  • total volume of applications – USD 40 million and EUR 21.4 million
  • the demand has been met in full.

Overall, based on results of 3–4 November2026, the volume of foreign currency offered within these transactions was more that three times the actual demand from banks.

FX market sustainability is the NBU’s constant goal

As provided for under the managed flexibility regime, the hryvnia exchange rate fluctuates in both directions: it not only weakens but also strengthens. Specifically, the official hryvnia exchange rate, calculated on 4 November for the following day, strengthened to USD/UAH 45.5, while the selling rate of the U.S. dollar in the cash segment of the foreign exchange market, as of the close of 4 November, reached USD/UAH 46.4.

The NBU stands ready to continue its efforts to maintain the sustainability of the foreign exchange market. Despite the absence of systemic problems with the physical availability of foreign currency cash in banks, the NBU plans to carry out such operations on 5 November as well. This precautionary step will keep the financial system’s FX cash liquidity sufficient to meet the needs of Ukrainians, should the need arise.

For reference

The NBU’s transactions to exchange banks’ non-cash foreign currency for cash foreign currency to replenish their foreign cash holdings do not affect the volume of Ukraine’s international reserves in any way.

item.title: NBU’s Position on Draft Law No. 10225-d on Virtual Asset Circulation
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine supports regulating the virtual asset market in Ukraine based on the European MiCA approach, international standards, and IMF recommendations.

Our fundamental position is that the development of this market must not pose a threat to Ukraine’s monetary sovereignty, price and financial stability, or economic security.

The NBU was actively involved in preparing Draft Law No. 10225-d. Within a working group that included members of parliament, the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC), market representatives, government agencies, and international partners, a number of important compromises were reached.

However, the drafting process was not sufficiently transparent. The NBU received the final version of the draft law, recommended by the relevant Verkhovna Rada Committee for approval in the second reading, only late yesterday evening. The final version does not reflect a number of fundamental agreements reached during the drafting process.

Today, NBU Deputy Governor Oleksii Shaban voiced the NBU’s concerns at a Committee meeting. However, the format of the discussion did not allow for a full-fledged professional debate. Therefore, the NBU is publicly highlighting three fundamental risks:

1. Uncontrolled admission of foreign tokens

The draft law allows foreign tokens to enter the Ukrainian market even if they effectively perform the functions of electronic money but are not subject to the relevant regulation and supervision in their countries of issuance.

This poses risks to monetary sovereignty, monetary policy transmission, payment infrastructure, and financial stability.

The NBU’s position: The NBU must have the authority to assess the risks associated with such foreign tokens and, where necessary, restrict their circulation in Ukraine, just as it can for tokens issued in Ukraine.

2. Regulatory gaps and unequal requirements

Simplified admission of foreign virtual assets must not allow them to circumvent the requirements established for comparable Ukrainian assets.

Otherwise, there is a risk of uncontrolled expansion of certain virtual assets and the emergence of market segments that would effectively remain outside adequate government oversight.

The NBU’s position: The rules governing the admission of foreign assets must prevent circumvention of regulatory requirements and regulatory arbitrage, while safeguarding monetary sovereignty and financial stability.

3. Risks of monopolization and corruption in the authorization process

Certain provisions of the draft law create risks of market monopolization and potential corruption in the authorization of participants by the NSSMC.

The NBU’s initial position was that there should be no quantitative restrictions on trading platform operators, provided they complied with the established requirements.

As a compromise, the NBU agreed to the NSSMC’s proposal to initially limit the number of such operators to three legal persons chosen through a competitive selection process.

However, the final version of the draft law does not establish a clear limit on the number of operators allowed to operate during the first five years. This decision is left entirely to the discretion of the NSSMC, without adequate antitrust safeguards.

The NBU’s position: The risks of market monopolization and potential corruption must be eliminated by ensuring clear and transparent authorization rules.

The bottom line

The development of the virtual asset market and the protection of monetary and financial stability are not mutually exclusive. However, sustainable development is possible only if clear rules, proper regulation, and effective risk oversight are in place.

The NBU has made significant efforts to find compromises and develop a balanced regulatory framework.

However, the failure to take the NBU’s fundamental concerns into account makes it impossible for the NBU to support draft Law No. 10225-d in its current version.

We call on members of parliament to further refine the document with the involvement of all participants in the legislative process and to take the above concerns into account.

The NBU stands ready to continue constructive cooperation within its mandate to support the development of an innovative market that will not pose risks to the credibility of the hryvnia, financial stability, or Ukraine’s economic security.

item.title: Ukraine’s Government Borrows Equivalent of almost UAH 401 Billion through Auctions to Sell Domestic Government Debt Securities since Early 2026, and almost UAH 2,428 Billion Total since Martial Law Was Imposed
item.description:
In January – October 2026, the government of Ukraine raised UAH 345,653.9 million, USD 452.0 million, and EUR 696.7 million by offering domestic government debt securities at auctions, and allocated UAH 313,058.2 million, USD 650.0 million, and EUR 557.8 million towards redemption of domestic government debt securities.

In total, from the onset of russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine through 31 October 2026, Ukraine’s government raised UAH 1,827,769.6 million, USD 11,243.3 million, and EUR 3,944.0 million through primary auctions and allocated UAH 1,308,212.5 million, USD 12,145.3 million, and EUR 3,479.2 million to redeem domestic government debt securities.  

Effective operation of the domestic debt market has been achieved through coordinated efforts by the Government of Ukraine and the NBU. Specifically, in 2025, the NBU has ensured settlements for auctions to place domestic government debt securities with simultaneous exchange for outstanding domestic government debt securities of another issue. This has expanded the ability of the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine to carry out asset-side operations to manage domestic debt.

In October, the maximum yield on domestic government debt securities offered at auctions was 16.75% per annum for hryvnia-denominated bonds. Domestic government debt securities denominated in U.S. dollars and euros were not placed in September.

As at 1 November 2026, legal persons’ portfolio of domestic government debt securities made an equivalent of UAH 1,138.1 billion in total.

Currency distribution of the portfolio: 

  • UAH 1,060,147.8 million
  • USD 1,035.3 million
  • EUR 611.4 million.

Individuals’ portfolio of domestic government debt securities made an equivalent of UAH 173.1 billion in total. Currency distribution of the portfolio:

  • UAH 105,549.1 million
  • USD 1,170.7     million
  • EUR 285.3 million.

Non-residents hold an equivalent of UAH 18.2 billion in domestic government debt securities. Currency distribution of the portfolio:

  • UAH 16,968.5 million
  • USD 15.0 million
  • EUR 10.0 million.

Below are the NBU Depository’s detailed statistics on war bonds offered through auctions, as of 1 November 2026

As before, primary dealers – the banks – hold the largest portfolio of war bonds.

The total portfolio of war bonds owned by legal persons (excluding banks) was equivalent to UAH 71.7 billion, as compared with UAH 87.0 billion a year ago.

Currency distribution of the war bonds portfolio held by business entities:

  • UAH 47,367.9 million or 22.2% of the total value of hryvnia-denominated war bonds
  • USD 346.0 million or 17.6% of the total value of U.S. dollar-denominated war bonds
  • EUR 170.2 million or 20.8% of the total value of euro-denominated war bonds.

The total portfolio of war bonds owned by individuals was equivalent to UAH 111.7 billion, as compared with UAH 76.1 billion as of 1 October 2026.

Currency distribution of the war bonds portfolio held by individuals:

  • UAH 52,002.1 million or 24.4% of the total value of hryvnia-denominated war bonds
  • USD 1052.1 million or 53.4% of the total value of U.S. dollar-denominated war bonds
  • EUR 235.9 million or 28.8% of the total value of euro-denominated war bonds.

Nonresidents held UAH 5,696.1 million, USD 13.1 million and EUR 10.0 million in war bonds.

In October 2026, the Ministry of Finance redeemed UAH 15,354.7 million of hryvnia war bonds.

Find out more about the military domestic government debt securities here. The table presents data at amortized face value. 

Everyone can purchase war bonds now and strengthen the financial resilience of Ukraine.

item.title: NBU Introduces New FX Market Indicator and Updates Approaches to Determining, Calculating, and Publishing Indicators for Ukraine’s Money and FX Markets
item.description:
The National Bank of Ukraine has revised approaches to determining, calculating, and publishing the Ukrainian Money Market and FX Market Indicators. These changes will improve the transparency, reliability, and representativeness of the Money Market and FX Market Indicators and align the NBU’s practices with best international standards and IOSCO principles.

First, the NBU has approved a new version of the Regulation On Establishing the Official Exchange Rate of the Hryvnia to Foreign Currencies, Calculating the Reference Hryvnia-to-U.S. Dollar Exchange Rate, the Reference Hryvnia-to-Euro Exchange Rate, and the Accounting Price of Investment Metals (hereinafter referred to as the “Regulation”).

 The Regulation provides as follows:

1. Introducing a new FX market indicator (benchmark) – the reference UAH/EUR exchange rate as of 12 p.m.

The indicator reflects a reliable, accurate, and representative value of the UAH/EUR exchange rate, calculated using the reference value of the UAH/USD exchange rate and an accurate and representative indicator of the USD/EUR exchange rate in the spot market.

The indicator will be calculated based on the reference UAH/USD exchange rate as of 12 p.m. and the average half-hourly BFIX USD/EUR quotation calculated during the specified time period from 10:30 a.m. to 12 p.m. Kyiv time.

The new indicator was developed in response to requests from market participants. This benchmark will be useful for customers who buy or sell euros in the domestic market. It can serve as a guide for determining exchange rates in transactions between banks and customers conducted in euros. In addition, this indicator will simplify the execution of forward transactions in euros, enabling market participants to settle such contracts more efficiently.

2. Revising the methodology for calculating the official exchange rate of the hryvnia against foreign currencies (excluding the U.S. dollar), SDRs, and the accounting price of investment metals.

The revised methodology provides for the application of approaches similar to those used to calculate the reference UAH/EUR exchange rate as of 12 p.m., specifically based on the official UAH/USD exchange rate and the average half-hourly BFIX quotation calculated during the specified time period from 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Kyiv time.

3. Daily publication of additional information regarding:

  • the number and volumes of the normalized set of transactions included in the calculation of the official UAH/USD exchange rate/the reference UAH/USD exchange rate
  • the minimum and maximum exchange rates for the base range of transactions used to calculate these indicators
  • and the calculation type (under normal or special conditions).

The new version of the Regulation approved by NBU Board Resolution No.125 On Approving the Regulation on Establishing the Official Exchange Rate of the Hryvnia to Foreign Currencies, Calculating the Reference Hryvnia-to-U.S. Dollar Exchange Rate, the Reference Hryvnia-to-Euro Exchange Rate, and the Accounting Price of Investment Metals dated 2 November 2026 takes effect on 4 November 2026, except for the provisions regarding the introduction of daily publication of additional information on transactions, which enter into force on 1 February 2027.

Second, amendments have been made to the Regulation On Calculating and Publishing the Ukrainian Overnight Index Average (UONIA).

In particular, the amendments provide for the daily publication of additional information regarding:

  • the number and volumes of the base range of transactions used for calculating UONIA
  • the minimum and maximum values of ​​the rates of the base range of transactions used for calculating UONIA
  • the UONIA calculation type (under normal or special conditions).

These and other technical changes were approved by NBU Board Decision  No. 397 On Amendments to the Regulation On Calculating and Publishing the Ukrainian Overnight Index Average (UONIA) dated 2 November 2026, which takes effect on 4 November 2026, except for the provisions regarding the introduction of daily publication of additional information on transactions, which enter into force on 1 February 2027.

For reference.

Said amendments were supported by the Oversight Council for Ukrainian Money Market and FX Market Indicators at its meetings on 29 August 2024 and 25 June 2025, as well as by the Money and Foreign Exchange Markets Contact Group at its meetings on 26 September 2024 and 31 October 2026, and were discussed with market participants during public consultations in May–June 2026.

item.title: Almost UAH 13.8 Billion Transferred for Defense Needs from NBU’s Special Fundraising Account in October 2026
item.description:
As of 1 November 2026, the balance in the special fundraising account the NBU opened to support the defense forces on 24 February 2022 makes over UAH 1.1 billion. Last month, over UAH 2.9 billion was received to the special account.

Nearly UAH 173.3 billion, in equivalent, was received in the special account since the full-scale invasion.

Money has been coming in from individuals and businesses of Ukraine and from all over the international community (including the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Poland, Switzerland, Norway, Australia, France, Canada, Bulgaria, Hong Kong, Lithuania, and many other countries).

That includes an equivalent of almost UAH 150.8 billion that was remitted from abroad in foreign currencies (U.S. dollars, euros, GB pounds, Canadian dollars, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen, Swiss francs, Polish zlotys, and Australian dollars).

Overall, since the start of the full-scale war, the NBU has allocated almost UAH 173 billion, including about UAH 13.8 billion in October 2026, to meet the needs of the defense forces, in particular:

  • almost UAH 1,785 million for the National Guard of Ukraine
  • UAH 1,700 million for the National Police of Ukraine ((UAH 50 million transferred on 20 October 2026)
  • over UAH 38,503 million for the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine
  • UAH 999.5 million for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine
  • over UAH 8,386 million for the State Service of Special Communication and Information Protection of Ukraine (UAH 40.8 million on 6 October 2026)
  • over UAH 156.2 million for the State Emergency Service of Ukraine
  • almost UAH 40.1 million for the NSDC of Ukraine
  • over UAH 233 million for the State Special Transport Service
  • almost UAH 909.2 million for the Security Service of Ukraine
  • over UAH 286.9 million for the needs of military units  (UAH 186.5 million of previously unused funds were returned)
  • almost UAH 1,492 million for the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine
  • over UAH 115,454 million for the Defence Procurement Agency (UAH 7,351 million on 2 October 2026, UAH 2,066 million on 13 October 2026, UAH 1,139 million on 19 October 2026, UAH 2,862 million on 27 October 2026, UAH 157,1 million on 28 October 2026).
  • over UAH 3,037 million for defense activities of the regional military administrations (UAH 69.7 million on 24 September 2026, and almost UAH 5 million on 29 September 2026). At the same time, almost UAH 5.4 million of previously unused funds were returned

As a reminder, donations for defense needs can be made by bank transfer as well as by card using the link.

For reference

Information on the special account is updated daily on the NBU’s website.

item.title: Businesses Report Cautious Economic Outlook – Business Outlook Survey in October
item.description:
Businesses reported cautious expectations for their economic performance in October. Intensified attacks on energy, production, storage and logistics infrastructure, the resumption of power cuts, rising fuel prices, restricted exports due to port blockades, and a shortage of skilled labor dampened companies’ economic activity. Sustained consumer demand, the bumper harvest, an ample supply of goods, and the establishment of new logistics routes remained growth drivers. This is evidenced by the business activity expectations index (BAEI), which the NBU calculates every month, apart from a forced break in March–May 2022. The business activity expectations index (BAEI) was 47.1 in October, down from 48.2 in September 2026 and 50.3 in October 2025.

Industrial companies took a restrained view of their economic performance, citing the destruction of production facilities, energy shortages, and constrained exports caused by port blockades, the sectoral index being 48.0 in October, compared to 51.0 in September and 48.8 in October 2025. In contrast to the previous month, respondents expected a drop in the number of new orders for products, including export orders, and in stocks of raw materials and supplies. At the same time, industrial companies continued to expect an increase in their manufactured goods volumes, albeit at a slower pace. Respondents reported dimmer expectations about the amount of unfinished products (unfulfilled orders) and finished goods stocks.

On the back of the ongoing suspension of state funding for road and infrastructure reconstruction, a shortage of skilled labor and seasonal factors, construction companies reported the most cautious economic outlook among all sectors, the sectoral index being 38.5 in October, compared to 48.8 in September and 53.3 in October 2025. Following seven months of optimism, respondents expected a noticeable drop in construction volumes, the number of new orders, and in purchases of raw materials and supplies. Construction companies said they intended to purchase fewer contractor services amid sustained growth in the cost of these services and dimmer expectations about contractors’ availability.

Trading companies have reported a restrained economic outlook for three months running, driven by ongoing damage to warehousing facilities and rising transport and storage costs, the sectoral index being 46.8 in October, compared to 45.9 in September and 54.3 in October 2025. Respondents expected a further decrease in their trade turnover and in purchases of goods for sale, albeit at a slightly slower pace. Companies continued to expect a drop in their stocks of goods for sale and said they intended to cut their trading margins further.

Due to the ongoing destruction of transport and warehousing facilities, higher fuel prices, and a shortage of skilled labor, services companies continued to report restrained expectations for their economic performance, the sectoral index being 47.4 in October, compared to 47.3 in September and 48.7 in October 2025. In contrast to the previous month, companies expected a decline in the amount of services provided. Furthermore, respondents expected a decrease in the number of new orders for services and in the amount of services that are being provided.

Respondents across most of the surveyed sectors continued to expect rapid growth in purchase prices / raw material and supplies prices, declaring intentions to raise their selling prices at a fast pace. Only services companies expected weaker growth in purchase prices and said they intended to raise their selling prices more slowly.

Labor market conditions were unstable. In contrast to the previous month, companies across all sectors said they intended to reduce their workforces, with the construction sector declaring the strongest intentions.

Background

This survey was carried out from 5 October through 22 October 2026. A total of 587 companies were polled. Of the companies polled, 41.9% are industrial companies, 26.9% services companies, 25.0% trading companies, and 6.1% construction companies; 31.2% of the respondents are large companies, 28.3% medium companies, and 40.5% small companies. Of the surveyed companies, 34.8% are both exporters and importers, 8.5% are exporters only, 17.5% are importers only, and 39.2% are neither exporters nor importers.

The findings presented reflect only the opinions of the respondents (top managers of companies), and should not be considered as NBU assessments.

The monthly business activity expectations index (BAEI) is a tool for conducting the latest assessments and detecting trends in economic development. It is calculated on the basis of surveys of Ukrainian real sector companies regarding changes in their performance compared to the previous month.

Monthly business activity expectations indices are calculated on the basis of respondents’ replies. These indices are as follows: sectoral indices (for each sector of the economy) and a composite index (describes the country’s economic performance over a month). A value of 50 corresponds to the neutral level. Index values above the neutral level indicate positive expectations.

Read more about the October 2026 survey in the Monthly Surveys of Companies Subsection of the Publications Section on the NBU’s official website.

The NBU posts monthly survey results in the open data format.

The results of the next (November 2026) survey will be published on the first business day of December 2026.
